Date  
Event  
12 October 2023  
Email from Performance Inspector, BR containing Minister’s request for 
urgent update to MBN Update 2 (refer to email sent to BR on 26 
September 2023). Email stated, “Our oﬃce would appreciate this request 
being brought to the attention of the AC OCC and an urgent update of the 
brieﬁng note be completed by cob today as today is the COTL end date”.  
12 October 2023  
AC Vanderbyl emails AC Connors, Dir Jacobsen and DCE McCarthy and 
states he spoke with the union and they have no intention to walk out of 
police stations, the Minister is comfortable with the due diligence and legal 
process, the lessors had not objected to the clause [at that time] and OCC 
will update the relevant MBN. AC Vanderbyl also stated, “it is important 
no regional member talk to the building owner during this ﬁnal negotiation 
period” (9:48am).  
12 October 2023  
AC Connors responds to AC Vanderbyl and states several points are not 
correct. AC Connors aﬃrms all contact with the owners will be through 
legal channels with OCC managing on behalf of the QPS and asks 
AC Vanderbyl to “note the expectation of government members when they 
were briefed on the proposal was that they wished for operations to be 
occurring from that site by May 2024”.  
12 October 2023  
Lessors’ solicitor emails NRF. Lessors take exception to the conditions 
placed on the COTL.  
12 October 2023  
NRF advise Ms Campbell of the response from the lessors’ solicitor and 
asks for QPS to advise them of their response, considering the risks 
previously outlined (12:06pm).  
Ms Campbell forwards the email to Dir Jacobsen, AC Vanderbyl and an 
OCC staﬀer.  
12 October 2023  
Following consultation with OCC members, Dir Jacobsen notiﬁed NRF of 
Departmental Approval for the COTL.  
The due diligence report from C&W was not completed prior to signing the 
COTL.  
12 October 2023  
NRF emails the lessors’ legal representative to advise of Departmental 
Approval stating “…the only reservation of rights is in relation to the 
negotiation of the lease documents which is also expressly contemplated 
in the COTL” (3:58pm).  
12 October 2023  
Dir Jacobsen emails Ms Campbell and an OCC staﬀer advising, “Andrea 
and I discussed this advice with the AC this afternoon, who noted the risk 
that the pre-lease assessment may recommend works that the landlord 
does not agree, during the lease negotiation. The AC accepted this risk and 
agreed to the approach detailed below and asked that NRF provide 
conﬁrmation by 5pm that the revised advice has been accepted”.  
13 October 2023  
Lessors’ solicitor conﬁrms the COTL is unconditional and binds both 
parties.

Post COTL becoming unconditional 
27 October 2023 
Due diligence report provided by Cushman & Wakeﬁeld identifying $6.5M

20 November 2023  
QPS Ministerial Service Unit seek dot points for the Department of Premier 
and Cabinet about Courier Mail article.  
23 November 2023  
OCC made aware that an Operations oﬃcer is meeting with the lessors 
every fortnight. AC Vanderbyl again advises BR that “only OCC is to be 
communicating with the owner.”  
16 March 2024  
OCC conducts a re-write of CBRC submission originally authored by BR.  
18 March 2024  
AC Vanderbyl advises DCE McCarthy of concerns around lease via CBRC 
submission “Urgent: CBRCiC Stones Corner.”  
7 May 2024  
OCC (allegedly) challenged by DCE McCarthy on views about Stones Corner 
and OCC engages “Primary Advisory” to review the COTL.  
23 May 2024  
Lessors’ solicitor emails NRF in response to lease negotiations and 
reiterates the COTL remains binding on all parties. The letter states the 
rent commencement date remains 12 July 2024.  
8 July 2024  
CBRC submission outcome received.  
2 August 2024  
Final Primary Advisory Report received. According to the Report, “the lease 
terms in the COTL may be in the order of 35-45% above market rental rates, 
and the incentive in the order of 70% below the market level. That is, the 
terms in the COTL are highly favourable to the Lessor relative to market 
commercial terms”.  
7 August 2024  
QPS receives a letter of demand from the lessors.  
16–21 August 2024  
EBN ‘Expenditure approval to secure a new lease at 433 Logan Rd, Stones 
Corner’ was submitted to Commissioner Gollschewski. Estimates show a 
cost of approximately $116M for a 15-year term and a total cost of 
approximately $240M if the eight-year option is taken up by QPS. The EBN 
to approve expenditure was signed by then Commissioner Gollschewski 
on 21 August 2024 noting “under the previous oﬃcer holder the QPS was 
bound to this lease transaction”.

Annexure 4 – Recommendations made to the QPS 
The CCC has made the following recommendations directly to the QPS:  
Recommendation 1 
• 
Conduct reviews or audits of leasing processes to examine compliance with proper policies, 
procedures and delegation frameworks. 
• 
Deliver updated training following process change to ensure relevant employees are informed.  
• 
Communicate the updated leasing process and QPS strategic leasing plan to all impacted 
employees to ensure awareness and compliance, including how the policy interacts with other 
mechanisms such as financial delegations, procurement and contract management, ministerial 
approval and Cabinet Budget Review Committee (CBRC) process. 
Recommendation 2  
• 
Undertake a comprehensive review of the Property and Planning team, to ensure its resourcing 
profile supports the full functions of the QPS. 
• 
Consider whether reviews of other areas of the QPS that were transitioned from the Public 
Safety Business Agency are required to ensure their resourcing profile supports service delivery 
and delegations are at an appropriate level. 
Recommendation 3 
• 
Update its Corporate Governance Manual to ensure it includes a definition for what matters 
may require urgent consideration. The QPS should maintain records of urgent considerations 
and consider conducting annual reviews or audits of these matters to determine if they 
appropriately met the relevant definition. 
Recommendation 4 
• 
Deliver education and awareness sessions for applicable staff appointed to new committees, 
including processes involved for a submission (including when Ministerial or CBRC approval is 
required), and expectations of the committee when making a submission. 
Recommendation 5 
• 
Ensure all employees with financial delegations complete financial delegation training when 
appointed (substantive or acting) to a role with financial delegations, with regular ongoing 
refresher training. 
Recommendation 6  
• 
Review other governance and management training courses available for staff to aid their 
development into senior roles, such as those provided by the Queensland Ombudsman, the 
Public Sector Commission and the Queensland Treasury Corporation. 
• 
Require all ELT members (substantive and acting) to complete the Company Directors Course 
and other governance and management training.  
• 
Consider providing regular refresher training to all senior staff on governance.

Recommendation 7 
• 
The QPS’s updated committee submission form template should be reviewed to include formal 
sign off, endorsement (by the responsible person or position submitting the paper) and 
comments by each committee member (including subject matter experts), and a requirement 
to attach proof of consultation with subject matter experts (as relevant). 
Recommendation 8 
• 
Include a regular review mechanism (at least annually) into the Corporate Governance Manual 
for each committee to ensure it remains fit for purpose and undertake internal audits of each 
committee’s activities to inform such reviews.   
Recommendation 9 
• 
Develop and implement an action plan to address systemic organisational culture issues.

Annexure 5 – The CCC’s corruption functions and public 
reporting 
The CCC’s corruption functions 
68. 
The CCC’s corruption functions are provided for in the CC Act.6 The CCC has, among its 
corruption functions, responsibility for raising standards of integrity and conduct in units of 
public administration (UPA) and ensuring that complaints involving suspected corruption are 
dealt with appropriately.  
69. 
One of the CCC’s primary responsibilities is to investigate matters that may involve corrupt 
conduct by, or involving, a person holding an appointment7 within a UPA in Queensland. The 
CCC has primary responsibility for dealing with complaints about corrupt conduct.8  
70. 
Importantly, the CCC’s corruption functions extend to corrupt conduct and to conduct liable to 
allow, encourage or cause corrupt conduct.9 They are as concerned with prevention as much 
as they are with detection, investigation and potential prosecutions. The corruption functions 
are directed to a main purpose of the CC Act: to continuously improve the integrity of, and to 
reduce the incidence of corruption in, the public sector,10 including by helping UPAs to deal 
effectively and appropriately with corruption by increasing their capacity to do so.11 
71. 
The CCC performs its corruption functions in several ways. These include taking responsibility 
for conducting and completing investigations, as well as offering advice and recommendations 
to a UPA on handling corruption complaints. Additionally, the CCC fulfils its functions by sharing 
information with the public, such as reports on specific investigations.12 This promotes 
transparency, reassures the public that corruption allegations are being properly addressed, 
and helps enhance the integrity of the public sector.13 
The CCC’s power to publicly report 
72. 
The CCC may report in the performance of its functions14 and may report on a corruption 
matter.15 The CC Act recognises that the CCC performs its corruption functions, in part, by 
providing information to the public by reporting,16 including in relation to particular 
investigations, to provide transparency about how it performs those functions,17 and to 
continuously improve the integrity of, and reduce the incidence of corruption in, the public 
sector.18 The CCC does not report publicly on every matter it investigates. Whether to do so 
requires it to weigh the considerations set out in the CC Act and to act consistently with its 
overriding obligation to act independently, impartially and fairly, having regard to the purposes 
of the Act and the importance of protecting the public interest.19

Annexure 8 – Human rights compatibility statement 
84. 
In deciding to prepare and publish a public report, the CCC is required by the Human Rights Act 
2019 (HR Act) to act and make decisions in a way that is compatible with human rights. When 
making decisions, it is required to consider human rights relevant to the decision.21  
85. 
The decision to prepare and publish a public report engage the right to privacy and reputation 22 
of any person who is identified or may be identifiable from the report. Any interference with 
the right to privacy and reputation is lawful, being authorised by sections 64 and 64A of the CC 
Act and is not arbitrary: the report focuses primarily on systemic issues and makes no finding 
about the conduct or culpability of any person. To the extent the decision limits that right, the 
CCC considers the limitation reasonable and demonstrably justifiable,23 having regard to the 
importance of the purposes the report serves, the measures taken to ensure fairness 
(including, the procedural fairness afforded, and the limits imposed by section 48B of the CC 
Act), and the public interest in accountability for the stewardship of public funds. 
86. 
The CCC also has considered the right to a fair hearing 24 and the rights in criminal 
proceedings.25 No criminal proceeding is in contemplation, and thereby section 32 is not 
engaged. As to a right to a fair hearing, this report does not limit it: the report, makes no finding 
about the conduct or culpability of any person, and does not determine, prejudge or pre-empt 
any question of individual liability, which is not a question for the CCC and is not addressed in 
this report. 
87. 
The CCC considers that the decision to publish this report is compatible with human rights.
